page: Vultr vhf-2c-4gb is a virtual server in the High Frequency Compute family, featuring an Intel x86_64 architecture with 2 shared vCPUs mapped to 1 physical core with 2 threads. The system is equipped with 4.0 GB of system memory, providing 2.0 GB of RAM per core. Local storage is bundled, consisting of a 128 GB NVMe SSD. The processor runs at a clock speed of 2.0 GHz and includes 16 MB of L3 cache, supporting instruction sets such as AVX, AES, BMI2, and FMA, though it lacks AVX-512 extensions.

Benchmark results indicate mixed performance characteristics. Single-threaded workloads perform relatively well, with stress-ng single-core CPU performance scoring in the average range at 1873.78 and single-threaded gzip compression showing strong performance at 32.63 GB/sec. However, multi-core and memory-intensive operations show clear limitations. The stress-ng multi-core performance of 3596.49 and Passmark CPU score of 4124.35 fall into the weak category. Memory bandwidth is a notable bottleneck, with uncached read and write speeds of 22.81 GB/sec and 12.89 GB/sec respectively, both ranking in the bottom 10%.

Due to its shared CPU allocation and constrained memory bandwidth, this server exhibits performance tradeoffs under sustained multi-threaded or memory-heavy workloads, as evidenced by its poor database operations score of 999.52. From a cost-efficiency perspective, the server offers a low-cost entry point with bundled NVMe storage, making it suitable for budget-conscious deployments. It is best fit for lightweight, single-threaded applications, basic web serving, development environments, and small-scale background tasks that do not require sustained multi-core execution.

While single-threaded performance is respectable—demonstrated by average stress-ng single-core scores and strong single-threaded gzip compression—the shared CPU allocation and memory architecture present clear performance tradeoffs. Multi-core CPU benchmarks, Passmark scores, and uncached memory bandwidth fall into the weak and poor categories, with database operations showing significant limitations. Qualitatively, this server represents a budget-friendly option for resource-light applications. It is best suited for basic web serving, lightweight single-threaded tasks, and development environments rather than memory-intensive or highly parallelized database workloads.
